Cs-137 is fixed at the frayed edges of illite and other micas, so the ratio of exchangeable to total Cs-137 should depend on those clay minerals. 17_importance found that the OSSL Kex model relies most on the Al–OH band near 3620 cm⁻¹, part of their signature. 18_aloh found that in Fukushima’s Lowland soils, the clay-mineral bands correlate negatively with clay, the reverse of OSSL. title: Inside the Cs-137 models
text:
Data and models
The Cs-137 ratio of 10_cs137 (log10 of exchangeable over total Cs-137), the current selection of Fukushima spectra, and the Cs137 study’s test set. Two models:

frozen OSSL: block 4 of the OSSL Kex model, frozen, with a ridge regression on its flattened output, as in 10_cs137. It is built with CutCNN and ridge_head from soilspecdl, so integrated gradients apply to it.
Fukushima only: the CNN from random weights, trained on the Fukushima training samples for 40 epochs at a maximum learning rate of 3·10⁻³, the Kex schedule of 03_kex, not tuned for the ratio.

Their test scores:

Clay-mineral bands and the ratio
The second-derivative depths of 18_aloh on the SNV spectra, and their Spearman correlation with the Cs-137 ratio, overall and by soil type, with clay and Kex for context. title: Inside the Cs-137 models
text:
Findings
The Fukushima-only CNN relies on the clay-mineral O–H region for the Cs-137 ratio. By integrated gradients, 11% of its importance lies in 3600–3700 cm⁻¹, more per cm⁻¹ than any other region. In the occlusion test, its most important window is centred at 3749 cm⁻¹, just above the clay-mineral O–H bands. The next are at 3669, 3629 and 3709 cm⁻¹, within them, and the fifth at 1069 cm⁻¹, in the Si–O region. Its test R² is 0.57 (r 0.76), with the Kex schedule, which was not tuned for the ratio.
The frozen-OSSL model relies on other regions. It draws 32% of its importance from 2000–2800 cm⁻¹ and 20% from 2800–3200 cm⁻¹, and only 3.6% from 3600–3700 cm⁻¹. Its five most important occlusion windows all lie between 2589 and 2789 cm⁻¹. The two models’ profiles correlate at 0.36. Its ridge head reads standardised block-4 features, which gives large weights to features with little variance. Weak, quiet regions such as 2000–2800 cm⁻¹ may get their importance this way. Its test R² is 0.64 (r 0.81), the same as in 10_cs137.
The clay-mineral bands relate to the Cs-137 ratio as fixation on clay minerals predicts. Deeper bands go with a smaller exchangeable fraction: Spearman −0.20 for the Al–OH band and −0.21 for the kaolinite band, over all 1,389 samples. The relation holds in the Lowland soils (−0.20 and −0.19, 907 samples) and in the Andosols (−0.27 and −0.26, 213 samples).
So the Cs-137 ratio does not show the reversal that clay shows. In the Lowland soils, the band depths correlate negatively with clay (−0.31 and −0.35), but negatively with the Cs-137 ratio too, as expected. The ratio itself correlates with clay at 0.12 in the Lowland soils and 0.04 overall, where fixation would predict a negative relation. The bands track the Cs-137 ratio as expected, and clay doesn’t. The odd one out in the Lowland soils is more likely the clay values, or clay amount as a measure of the fixing minerals, than the bands. That is an interpretation of these correlations, not a test.
Kex correlates with the Cs-137 ratio at −0.49 in the 66 Peat soils, −0.42 in the 46 Red yellow soils and −0.22 in the 138 Forest soils, and near 0 in the Lowland soils and Andosols.

title: Paired spectra
text:
Findings
376 soils have both Bruker and Thermo spectra after the exclusions. 316 of them are Kazu samples, which are outside the sample selection of 03_kex and 04_cec. Which Bruker instrument and accessory measured them is not known yet.
The two instruments record the same soils at very different contrast. The Bruker spectra have a mean absorbance of 1.92 and a mean within-spectrum standard deviation of 0.40. The Thermo spectra have 0.51 and 0.066: about six times less contrast. SNV removes a difference of scale and offset, but not a non-linear one. Such a large difference in contrast suggests a difference in measurement mode or sample preparation, such as dilution, particle size or the accessory, more than a difference between spectrometers.
The spectral shapes of the same soil differ. The median correlation between a soil’s Bruker and Thermo spectra is 0.27 for raw and SNV spectra. After the first derivative it is 0.78, because the derivative removes the broad baseline differences.
Across soils, the instruments disagree most between 650 and 1300 cm⁻¹, the region of the Si–O bands of quartz and clay minerals. There, the correlation between instruments over the soils is 0.10 with SNV and 0.43 with the derivative. In the water bands, 1300–2000 and 3500–3950 cm⁻¹, it is about 0.6. In diffuse reflectance, the bands in this mineral region are the most sensitive to particle size and dilution.
Wavenumber calibration and resolution are minor. The best alignment shifts the Thermo bands by 1.6 cm⁻¹ and raises the correlation of the mean derivative spectra from 0.805 to 0.809. Smoothing the Bruker spectra by a Gaussian of up to 6 cm⁻¹ lowers the derivative mismatch by about 10%. Smoothing the Thermo spectra lowers it by about 3%. The Bruker bands are slightly narrower.
In a PCA fitted on OSSL, both instruments’ spectra of these soils sit within OSSL’s 99th percentiles of T² and Q. The Thermo spectra sit further from the OSSL mean on PC2: -1.40 standard deviations, against -1.01 for the Bruker spectra.
The OSSL models transfer better from the Bruker spectra, but not well. For CEC, zero-shot prediction from the Bruker spectra gives a correlation of 0.66 and an R² of 0.24. From the Thermo spectra of the same soils it gives 0.53 and -0.51. The bias is +2.0 cmolc/kg from Bruker and +5.1 from Thermo. For Kex, both instruments fail (correlation 0.19 and 0.15). The instrument explains part of the CEC gap. The rest, and most of the Kex gap, comes from these soils or their preparation, which OSSL does not cover, or from the Bruker instrument differing from the instruments behind OSSL.
Questions for the Fukushima data team follow from this: the accessory of each instrument, whether the samples were diluted (for example with KBr) or measured neat, and how finely they were ground.

ParamStats records, every every training steps and for each parameter tensor:

weight: the norm ‖W‖;
grad: the norm of the gradient;
update: the size of this step relative to the weights, ‖ΔW‖/‖W‖;
moved: how far the weights are from where the fit started, ‖W − W₀‖/‖W₀‖.

A relative update near 10⁻³ is a common rule of thumb for a layer that learns at a sensible rate. Much smaller means the layer barely learns, and much larger means it is unstable.
Adam scales each element’s step by the history of its own gradients, so the step per element is similar across layers. The default initialisation sets a layer’s weights to a scale of about 1/√(fan-in), the number of inputs to each unit. So with the same learning rate, ‖ΔW‖/‖W‖ grows with √(fan-in). In SpectralCNN, the fan-in of the 5 convolutions is 3, 48, 96, 192 and 384. A smaller relative update in block 1 is therefore expected, and doesn’t by itself mean that block 1 learns less.



ParamStats
def ParamStats(
    every:int=10
):
Record the norm, gradient norm, relative update and relative distance from the start of each parameter, every every steps


tracked_fit trains learn with a one-cycle schedule while recording ParamStats and fastai’s ActivationStats. title: Training dynamics
text:
Findings
The CNN trains without the usual optimisation problems in all three runs. Gradients reach block 1. Activations neither collapse nor saturate. No channel of any block is dead (above 0.05 for less than 1% of spectra and positions) or linear (above 0.05 for more than 99%), on OSSL or on Fukushima spectra. At their peak, the relative updates of the convolutions in blocks 2 to 5 are 1–3·10⁻³ on OSSL (learning rate 10⁻³) and 2–4·10⁻³ on Fukushima (learning rate 3·10⁻³). Block 1’s are several times smaller, for the reason in the next paragraph. In all three runs the updates fall to a few 10⁻⁶ at the end of the one-cycle schedule.
The differences between blocks in update size follow the initialisation, not the learning. In the first OSSL epoch, the relative updates of blocks 1 to 5 are in the ratio 1 : 4.2 : 5.7 : 8.1 : 11.3. The square roots of their fan-ins are in the ratio 1 : 4 : 5.7 : 8 : 11.3. How far each layer moves by the end of OSSL pretraining also rises from block 1 to block 5, but less steeply: 1 : 1.75 : 2.5 : 3.8 : 5.4. The initialisation explains part of why block 1 moves least, so that alone doesn’t show that block 1 learns less.
Block 5 becomes sparse during training. Its share of activations ≤ 0.05 rises from 0.52 to 0.79 during OSSL pretraining, and from 0.53 to 0.72 when training on Fukushima from random weights. At the end, 15–17% of its activations are above 2.5, against at most 3.4% in blocks 1 to 4. Each of its channels responds strongly at a few positions and is off elsewhere. The global average pool then averages those positions.
Fine-tuning keeps the weights close to the pretrained ones. The convolutions and head move 0.03 to 0.29 of their norm, against 0.24 to 1.91 during pretraining from random weights. Compared with training from random weights, which runs twice as many epochs, fine-tuning moves each layer 0.44 to 0.58 as far. No layer takes a clearly larger share of the change.
In the first epoch of fine-tuning, the median gradient norm of block 1 is 0.21. At the end of OSSL pretraining it was 0.080, 2.6 times smaller. For the other layers the ratio is 1.6 to 2.2. This hints that the mismatch between OSSL and Fukushima is largest near the input, but the evidence is weak: the two gradients are measured at different points of different schedules.
On Fukushima, the training loss keeps falling after the validation loss levels off. When fine-tuning, the training loss halves from epoch 10 to epoch 19 (0.035 to 0.017) while the validation loss stays at 0.039–0.040. On OSSL, the validation R² still rises from 0.67 at epoch 10 to 0.79 at epoch 19. The test scores of the two Fukushima runs (R² 0.38 and 0.43) are close to the means in 03_kex (0.37 and 0.42).
These diagnostics find no fault in how the network trains. They can’t show whether it learns the right features for Fukushima. The CKA comparison and linear probes of 07, and the wavenumber importance of 08, address that.

title: OSSL to Fukushima transfer
text:
WarningWork in progress



The findings change as new experiments run and as the Fukushima data team answers the questions below.
This project tests whether CNN models of soil mid-infrared (MIR) spectra, trained on the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL), help predict soil properties from spectra of Fukushima soils. OSSL was measured on Bruker instruments and the Fukushima soils on a Thermo Nicolet. The targets are exchangeable potassium (Kex), cation exchange capacity (CEC) and the ratio of exchangeable to total Cs-137. The Fukushima data are 1,389 soil samples from 391 fields, sampled from 2013 to 2020.
The audience is soil scientists working with the Fukushima data and anyone transferring spectral models between instruments. Each notebook asks one question. The table under “Notebooks” gives each question and its answer. The questions under “Questions for the Fukushima data team” need answers from the people who sampled and measured the soils.

title: OSSL to Fukushima transfer
text:
Findings
OSSL models fail on the Fukushima spectra without retraining. Without fine-tuning, the OSSL Kex model gives R² below 0 and a correlation of 0.13 on the Fukushima test samples. The OSSL CEC model gives a correlation of 0.57, with a large bias.
Trained on Fukushima labels, OSSL helps Kex a little on fields already seen in training, and not at all on new fields. On the Cs137 study’s test samples, full fine-tuning gives Kex R² 0.41 against 0.37 for a CNN trained on Fukushima only. For CEC it gives 0.74 against 0.71. When whole fields are held out, ridge regression on frozen OSSL features gives Kex R² 0.26 against 0.28 for ridge regression on the spectra.
For the Cs-137 ratio, frozen OSSL features help on new fields, but only slightly. All three models below use ridge regression, scored with folds grouped by field; only the input changes. Ridge on the preprocessed spectra (SNV, then a Savitzky-Golay first derivative) gives R² 0.52. Ridge on the activations of block 4 of the two CNNs trained on OSSL to predict Kex and CEC, with their weights frozen, gives R² 0.57. Ridge on block 4 of the same CNNs with random weights gives R² 0.52, the same as the spectra. The gain of 0.05 (bootstrap interval over fields 0.017 to 0.077) therefore comes from what the networks learned on OSSL, not from the network architecture. It cuts the unexplained variance from 48% to 43%.
Scores on the Cs137 study’s split are optimistic. 89% of its 398 test samples come from a field that also has samples in training. Holding out whole fields lowers Kex R² by 0.10 to 0.13 and the Cs-137 ratio by 0.05 to 0.08.
The OSSL soils cover the Fukushima soils in property space. The OSSL Kex model predicts the closest OSSL soil to each Fukushima soil at R² 0.60. Removing the Bruker-Thermo difference from the spectra, and augmenting the spectra during pretraining, both left its Kex correlation on the Fukushima spectra near 0. Water vapour and sample moisture do not explain the failure.
In Fukushima’s Lowland soils, the sharp clay-mineral bands near 3620 and 3695 cm⁻¹ relate to clay in the opposite direction to OSSL. Band depth is measured in each spectrum as minus the minimum of its second derivative near the band centre. In the Lowland soils, deeper bands go with less clay (Spearman -0.31 and -0.35, 631 samples). In the OSSL soils with the closest lab properties, deeper bands go with more clay (0.28 and 0.39). The OSSL Kex model relies most on this region, so this is one sign that OSSL’s spectral relations do not hold in Fukushima soils. It has not been shown to cause the Kex failure.
On new fields, Kex can hardly be predicted within paddy fields. Ridge regression on the spectra gives R² -0.03 in paddy fields and 0.20 in upland fields. Paddy fields hold 880 of the 1,388 samples with Kex.

section: Questions for the Fukushima data team
text:
Questions for the Fukushima data team

Fields: does each field_no name the same field in every year? 20_grouped_cv assumes it does.
Potassium fertilisation: which fields received extra K after 2011 to limit Cs-137 uptake, and from when? Added K leaves no mineral signature in the spectra. If the paddy fields received it, that would explain why the spectra cannot rank Kex within paddy fields.
Kex method: is soil_ex_K2O in mg K₂O per 100 g of dry soil, and which extraction gave it? OSSL uses 1 M ammonium acetate at pH 7. The project assumes mg K₂O per 100 g and divides by 47.1 to get cmolc/kg.
Other units: are soil_MgO and soil_CaO in mg of oxide per 100 g of dry soil, and soil_C and soil_N in %? The comparisons with OSSL in 12_wetchem depend on these conversions.
Clay: which method measured clay, and does it differ between soil types or years? If the clay values in the Lowland soils are suspect, the comparisons in 12_wetchem, 18_aloh and 19_cs137_inside need revisiting.
Clay mineralogy: which clay minerals dominate the Lowland paddy soils? Do mineralogy data, such as XRD or oxalate-extractable Al and Si, exist for any samples? If the mineralogy is unusual, models trained on Fukushima labels are the way forward rather than OSSL.
Sample preparation: how were the samples dried, ground and, if at all, diluted for each instrument? Did the Bruker and Thermo scans of the paired soils use the same prepared material? The answers decide which spectral corrections are realistic.
Instruments: which accessory, resolution and purging did the Thermo Nicolet use? Which Bruker instrument and accessory measured the paired soils?
Doubtful scans: 00_data leaves out 12 samples whose scans disagree between operators or between file exports. Which scans are right? The answer can bring these samples back.

title: Cs-137 ratio
text:
Findings
Frozen layers of the OSSL models predict the Cs-137 ratio clearly better than the spectra. On the 341 test samples of the current selection, a ridge regression on block 4 of the OSSL Kex model gives a test R² of 0.64 (r 0.80), and on block 4 of the Kex and CEC models together 0.65 (r 0.81). The best layer is block 5 of the two models together, at 0.66 (r 0.81). On the same samples, PLSR on the .spa spectra gives 0.56 (r 0.76) and a ridge regression on them 0.54. Neither OSSL model was trained on the Cs-137 ratio.
Part of the gain comes from the architecture, not from OSSL. Block 4 of the model with random weights gives 0.61, against 0.64 for the OSSL Kex model. The OSSL features add most when the training samples are few: with 200 samples, block 4 gives 0.49 for the OSSL Kex model, 0.43 for the random model and 0.40 for the spectra. With all 1,048, they give 0.64, 0.61 and 0.54.
With 400 training samples, a ridge regression on block 4 of the OSSL models (0.57 to 0.59) beats a ridge regression on the spectra with all 1,048 (0.54). Like Kex in 08_learning_curve, every set of features is still gaining at 1,048 samples, by 0.03 to 0.04 R² from 700 samples.
As for Kex, the pooled features transfer worst: 0.48 for the OSSL Kex model and 0.54 for the OSSL CEC model, no better than the spectra.
PLSR on the Cs137 study’s own spectra gives 0.54 on its full split (1,194 training and 398 test samples) and 0.56 on the samples of the current selection. So the smaller selection doesn’t lower the scores. These PLSR scores are below the R² of about 0.68 that the earlier study reported for PLSR and Cubist on a Kennard-Stone split.
None of the three Kennard-Stone splits reproduces the test set of the study’s files. They share 166 to 189 of its 398 test samples, against about 100 expected by chance. So the split behind the study’s files is closer to Kennard-Stone than to random, but was made with other inputs or settings.
On the Kennard-Stone splits, PLSR on the study’s spectra gives 0.56 to 0.62, the best on the split made on SNV and first-derivative spectra. That is higher than the 0.54 on the files’ split, but still below 0.68. The split explains part of the earlier study’s score. Its preprocessing or Cubist may explain the rest.
On the same splits, the ridge regressions on frozen layers give 0.68 to 0.71. Block 4 of the OSSL Kex and CEC models together gives 0.70 to 0.71 (r 0.84 to 0.85), and PLSR on the .spa spectra gives 0.57 to 0.64. So the frozen OSSL features reach or exceed the earlier study’s 0.68 on a comparable kind of split. Block 4 of the random model gives 0.67 to 0.68, so most of the gain over PLSR comes from the convolutional features with a ridge regression, and OSSL adds 0.01 to 0.04. These regressions are scored on the 329 to 335 test samples of each split in the current selection. PLSR on the study’s spectra is scored on all 398.

title: Block 4 transfer
text:
Variants
The variants use soilspecdl’s CutCNN, which keeps the first blocks of a SpectralCNN and adds a new head. Its head reads either the average of the last block’s output over positions (flat=False), as SpectralCNN does, or all channels at all positions (flat=True), which keeps band position. soilspecdl’s ridge_head fits a ridge regression from a model’s frozen features to the targets, and copies it into the head. Fine-tuning then starts from a head that already reads the frozen features well, instead of from a random one.
reset_top keeps all blocks but gives block 5 and the head new random weights:

title: Block 4 transfer
text:
Findings
No fine-tuned starting point beats the frozen reference. With 1,047 training samples, the ridge regression on block 4 gives a test R² of 0.43 (r 0.66). The best fine-tuned model is the whole pretrained model, at 0.41 (r 0.65). With 400 samples, the ridge regression gives 0.35, and the best fine-tuned model is the flattened cut with a ridge head, at 0.32.
Fine-tuning the flattened cut with a ridge head lowers its score. Before fine-tuning, it predicts exactly what the reference predicts: its head is the same ridge regression on the same features and samples. After fine-tuning, it scores 0.38 with 1,047 samples and 0.31 to 0.32 with 400, at either learning rate. With 1,047 samples, it ends level with resetting block 5 (0.38). The two differ from the reference in the samples they see: the ridge head is fitted on all drawn samples, and fine-tuning trains on 90% of them. That alone is unlikely to explain a drop of 0.05.
On block 4, keeping band position matters. A new head on all channels and positions of block 4 gives 0.37 with 1,047 samples. A new head on their average over positions gives 0.23. With 400 samples, the two give 0.29 and 0.14. Averaging block 4’s output over positions loses much of its Kex information.
Block 5’s pretrained weights help fine-tuning. Resetting block 5 and the head gives 0.38 with 1,047 samples, against 0.41 for the whole pretrained model. So block 5 is specific to OSSL as a frozen layer, as 07_inside_transfer found, but it is still a better starting point than random weights.
The higher learning rate, 3·10⁻³, is better for every starting point except the ridge head, where the two rates give the same result within the spread over seeds.
With these schedules, the best use of the pretrained model on Fukushima Kex is as a frozen feature extractor read by a ridge regression on block 4, not as a starting point for fine-tuning. Fine-tuning moves the model away from a readout that is already better than what it learns.

12_wetchem and 16_moisture found that the OSSL Kex model fails on the Fukushima spectra, not on the soils, and that the Thermo spectra carry a shift of intensity from below 2000 cm⁻¹ to 2800–3700 cm⁻¹. The model also fails on the Bruker spectra of the same soils, which show little of that shift. This notebook asks which wavenumbers the models rely on, to see where OSSL and Fukushima differ in what matters for Kex.
Three methods, so that no single method decides: integrated gradients, occlusion, and ridge coefficients. The module part uses small random arrays, so it runs without the data. The sections from Data and models onwards read OSSL and the Fukushima data, and are marked #| fukudata.

title: Wavenumber importance
text:
Methods
integrated_gradients attributes each prediction to the wavenumbers (Sundararajan et al. 2017). It works on the spectra after BatchSNV, as the model sees them, and integrates the gradient along the straight path from a flat spectrum of zeros to the spectrum, with steps points of the midpoint rule. The attributions of a spectrum sum to its prediction minus the prediction for the flat spectrum, up to the error of the integration:



integrated_gradients
def integrated_gradients(
    model, # Trained `SpectralCNN`
    X, # Preprocessed spectra, one per row, as passed to `predict`
    steps:int=32, # Number of points on the path
    bs:int=128, # Batch size
)->numpy.ndarray: # One attribution per spectrum and wavenumber
Integrated gradients of the predictions of model for X, from a flat spectrum of zeros



rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X_syn = rng.normal(size=(6, len(shared_wns)))
m_syn = SpectralCNN().eval()
ig = integrated_gradients(m_syn, X_syn, steps=64)
xs = torch.as_tensor(BatchSNV()(TensorSpectrum(torch.tensor(X_syn, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1), wns=shared_wns))).float()
with torch.no_grad(): delta = (m_syn(xs) - m_syn(torch.zeros_like(xs))).numpy()
test_close(ig.sum(1), delta, eps=0.05 * np.abs(delta).max())

occlusion flattens one window of width wavenumbers at a time, setting the preprocessed spectra to zero there, and measures how much the mean squared error against y rises. It needs no gradients:



occlusion
def occlusion(
    model, # Trained `SpectralCNN`
    X, # Preprocessed spectra, one per row
    y, # Targets
    width:int=20, # Window width, in points
)->pandas.DataFrame: # One row per window: its centre wavenumber and the rise in mean squared error
Rise in mean squared error of model when each window of width points of X is set to zero



occ = occlusion(m_syn, X_syn, np.zeros(6), width=200)
test_eq(len(occ), int(np.ceil(len(shared_wns) / 200)))

title: Wavenumber importance
text:
Findings
On OSSL, the OSSL Kex model relies most densely on the 3600–3700 cm⁻¹ region, the Al–OH stretching bands of illite, smectite and kaolinite near 3620 cm⁻¹. By integrated gradients, that 100 cm⁻¹ region holds 10% of the importance, more per cm⁻¹ than any other region. Flattening the 40 cm⁻¹ window centred at 3629 cm⁻¹ raises the error more than any other window. Overall, 64% of the importance lies below 2000 cm⁻¹: 38% between 650 and 1300 cm⁻¹ and 26% between 1300 and 2000 cm⁻¹. For Kex, an illite band is a plausible thing to rely on, since illite holds K. That reading is a hypothesis about the model, not a result.
On the Fukushima spectra, the same model spreads its importance differently. The share of 3600–3700 cm⁻¹ falls from 10% to 5.7%, and the share of 650–1300 cm⁻¹ from 38% to 28%. The share of 2000–3200 cm⁻¹ rises from 13% to 23%. In the occlusion test on Fukushima, the window that matters most is centred at 3749 cm⁻¹, with 3629 cm⁻¹ second. The correlation between the model’s profiles on OSSL and on Fukushima is 0.66.
The models trained on Fukushima differ from the OSSL model. The fully fine-tuned model’s profile on Fukushima correlates at 0.69 with the OSSL model’s on OSSL. It keeps 10% of its importance in 3600–3700 cm⁻¹. The Fukushima-only model correlates at 0.48. It gives 6.8% to 3600–3700 cm⁻¹ and 18% to 2000–2800 cm⁻¹, against 6.8% for the OSSL model on OSSL. Its most important occlusion windows are centred at 3709, 2829 and 1589 cm⁻¹.
The ridge coefficients are not a usable importance measure here. The OSSL and Fukushima ridge profiles correlate at 0.09, and with the integrated-gradient profiles at 0.05 to 0.20. Neighbouring wavenumbers are strongly correlated, so ridge spreads its weight over them in ways that change from one dataset to the other.
These results connect with 16_moisture. Between 3450 and 3700 cm⁻¹, the Thermo spectra are higher than their OSSL analogues by 0.87 after SNV, in 99% of the pairs. A broad absorption there could hide the sharp Al–OH band that the OSSL model relies on most. Measuring the 3620 cm⁻¹ band height in both datasets, and its relation to Kex in each, would test this. This notebook doesn’t.

pretrain calls soilspecdl’s train_or_load with the project’s grid, shared_wns, and weights folder, model_dir(). It splits OSSL at random into 90% training and 10% validation, and trains for epochs one-cycle epochs, as in the soilspecdl quick start. It saves the weights and the training history in model_dir(). A later call with the same fname loads them instead of training again. Delete the files to train again. Training on an Apple silicon GPU (MPS) is not fully deterministic, even with a fixed seed.

fit_models
def fit_models(
    pretrained, # Model returned by `pretrain`
    X, # Preprocessed Fukushima spectra
    y, # Targets
    is_test, # True for the samples of the fixed test set
    seed:int=0, # Seed for the validation split and the training
    epochs:int=20, # Training epochs after the first, frozen, epoch of fine-tuning
    lr:float=0.001, # Maximum learning rate
    schedules:NoneType=None, # Model name: (epochs, maximum learning rate), for 'fully fine-tuned' and 'Fukushima only'
)->dict: # Model name: test predictions
Test predictions of the models in model_names


The six models see the same validation split. The trained models see the same number of epochs:

Zero-shot predicts with the pretrained model as it is.
Zero-shot AdaBN predicts with the pretrained model after adabn has recomputed its BatchNorm statistics on the non-test Fukushima spectra. It uses no Fukushima targets.
Head only trains the pretrained head, a linear layer of 257 weights, for epochs + 1 epochs. The backbone weights stay fixed, including the BatchNorm scale and shift. The BatchNorm running statistics still update to the Fukushima batches during training.
Fine-tuned uses fastai’s fine_tune: one epoch with the backbone frozen at learning rate lr, then epochs epochs of the whole model. In that second phase the head’s maximum learning rate is lr / 2, and the backbone’s is lr / 200. With lr=1e-3, the backbone trains at most at 5e-6, 200 times lower than the Fukushima-only model, and stays close to its pretrained weights.
Fully fine-tuned trains the whole pretrained model with the schedule of the Fukushima-only model: epochs + 1 one-cycle epochs at maximum learning rate lr. It differs from the Fukushima-only model only in its starting weights.
Fukushima only trains a SpectralCNN from random weights for epochs + 1 epochs.

schedules gives the fully fine-tuned and Fukushima-only models their own number of one-cycle epochs and maximum learning rate, such as ones chosen with cv_curves and cv_final below. Without it, both use the defaults above.
With an untrained model in place of a pretrained one and one epoch, each model predicts the 20 test samples:

preds_syn = fit_models(SpectralCNN(), X_syn, y_syn, is_test_syn, epochs=1)
test_eq({k: v.shape for k, v in preds_syn.items()}, {k: (20,) for k in model_names})

Joint training
Fine-tuning trains on OSSL first and on Fukushima afterwards. Joint training uses both at once: one model trains from random weights on all OSSL spectra and the Fukushima training samples together. The Fukushima samples are repeated so that they make up about share of the training samples. Without repetition, they would be under 2% of them. Validation and test use Fukushima samples only, as in fuku_dls:

    yo, # OSSL targets
    Xf, # Preprocessed Fukushima spectra
    yf, # Fukushima targets

    valid_pct:float=0.1, # Share of the Fukushima training samples used for validation

title: Sample moisture
text:
Findings
Compared with their OSSL soil analogues, the Fukushima spectra differ by a broad, systematic shift of intensity between regions. After SNV, Fukushima is higher between 2800 and 3700 cm⁻¹ in almost every pair: by 0.62 on average between 2800 and 3200 cm⁻¹, 0.79 in the O–H stretching band (3200–3450 cm⁻¹) and 0.87 between 3450 and 3700 cm⁻¹, in 99 to 100% of the pairs. It is lower below 2000 cm⁻¹: by 0.43 between 650 and 1300 cm⁻¹ and 0.65 between 1300 and 1610 cm⁻¹, in 84 to 98% of the pairs. The 1,385 pairs use 831 distinct OSSL analogues.
This pattern doesn’t look like water in the samples. Water would raise both water bands. The O–H stretching band is higher than in the analogue for 99.9% of the Fukushima soils (median height 2.64 against 1.72), but the H–O–H bending band is higher for only 4.7% (median 0.45 against 0.59). SNV makes every difference relative: a large rise in one region lowers the rest after normalisation. So a lower bending band doesn’t rule out some water, but the two bands don’t move together as water would make them.
Neither band explains the Kex errors. Their Spearman correlations with the zero-shot error of the OSSL model, and with the residuals of the fully fine-tuned and Fukushima-only models, are at most 0.14 in absolute value. The largest are for the excess over the analogue, with the fine-tuned model’s residuals (0.14 for both bands). By quarters of the O–H stretching band, the zero-shot correlation is −0.03, 0.10, 0.27 and 0.16, without a steady trend.
The systematic shift towards the 2800–3700 cm⁻¹ region, present in nearly every Fukushima spectrum, is the largest difference from matched OSSL soils found so far. It fits a difference in measurement mode or sample preparation, such as particle size, dilution or the accessory, which changes the relative intensity of strong and weak bands. That is an interpretation, not a test. A shift that is the same in every spectrum adds a constant to a linear model’s predictions and leaves their ranking unchanged. The analogue EPO in 13_epo estimated its directions from uncentred pair differences, so they include this shift, and removing them did not give the ridge regression a usable correlation. A CNN is not linear, so the shift can change its ranking. This notebook doesn’t test that.
The shift comes mainly from the Thermo measurement. For the 375 soils with both Bruker and Thermo spectra and all seven properties, the Thermo spectra show the shift against their OSSL analogues even more strongly than the current selection: +1.29 in the O–H stretching band and −1.84 between 650 and 1300 cm⁻¹, in 99 to 100% of the pairs. The Bruker spectra of the same soils, against the same analogues, show a much weaker shift towards high wavenumbers: +0.21 in the O–H stretching band (higher in 81% of the pairs), and +0.12 between 650 and 1300 cm⁻¹, the opposite sign to Thermo. 316 of these soils are Kazu samples, outside the current selection. Whether the two instruments measured the same prepared material is not known.
The OSSL Kex model fails zero-shot on these Bruker spectra too (correlation 0.19, 05_paired), although they show little of the shift. So the shift is not the whole cause of the Kex failure.

12_wetchem and 13_epo found that the zero-shot failure lies in the Fukushima spectra, and that linear corrections don’t fix it. Augmentation takes the other route: it trains the CNN on OSSL spectra perturbed in the ways that 05_paired measured between instruments, so that the features it learns change less under such differences.
The perturbations act on raw absorbance, before SNV and the derivative. So in training, SNV and the derivative run on each batch, after the perturbations. At prediction, the spectra are preprocessed offline as before.

Preprocessing on batches
SNVDeriv applies SNV, then the Savitzky-Golay filter, to each spectrum of a batch, as preprocessings()['snv_d1'] does offline. The filter is linear, so it is a matrix: filtering the rows of an identity matrix with SciPy gives it, edges included, and a matrix product applies it on the GPU.

    n, # Number of wavenumbers
    window_length:int=15, # As in `SavitzkyGolay`
    polyorder:int=3, # As in `SavitzkyGolay`

title: Augmentation
text:
Perturbations
SpectralAug perturbs raw absorbance spectra of training batches. Each perturbation applies to each spectrum with probability p, with a random size drawn from its range:

Gaussian broadening with a standard deviation up to sigma points. On the 2 cm⁻¹ grid, 3 points is 6 cm⁻¹, the largest broadening tested in 05_paired.
A shift along the wavenumber axis of up to shift points, by linear interpolation. 05_paired measured 1.6 cm⁻¹, or 0.8 points.
A contrast change: absorbance, clipped at 10⁻³, raised to a power between gamma[0] and gamma[1], drawn on a log scale. 05_paired found about six times less contrast in the Thermo spectra, which SNV does not fully remove.
A baseline: a constant, a slope and a curvature across the spectrum, each up to baseline times the spectrum’s standard deviation.
Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of noise times the spectrum’s standard deviation.

Scaling a whole spectrum is left out, because SNV removes it. As a fastai transform with split_idx = 0, it leaves validation batches unchanged.



SpectralAug
def SpectralAug(
    p:float=0.5, # Probability of each perturbation, per spectrum
    sigma:float=3.0, # Largest Gaussian broadening, in points
    shift:float=1.0, # Largest shift, in points
    gamma:tuple=(0.5, 2.0), # Range of the contrast exponent
    baseline:float=0.2, # Largest baseline term, relative to the spectrum's standard deviation
    noise:float=0.005, # Noise standard deviation, relative to the spectrum's standard deviation
):
Random broadening, shift, contrast, baseline and noise of raw absorbance spectra, on training batches only



aug = SpectralAug()
set_seed(0)
xa = aug(xb, split_idx=0)
test_eq((type(xa), xa.shape), (TensorSpectrum, xb.shape))
test_eq(torch.allclose(xa, xb), False)
test_eq(torch.equal(aug(xb, split_idx=1), xb), True)
test_close(SpectralAug(p=0)(xb, split_idx=0), xb, eps=1e-5)

text:
Findings
Augmentation during OSSL pretraining doesn’t make the CNN transfer to Fukushima. The augmented model reaches an OSSL validation R² of 0.78, against 0.79 without augmentation. Its zero-shot correlation for Fukushima Kex is -0.10 on the test samples, against 0.13 without augmentation. Its bias is smaller (0.14 against 0.29 in log1p units), and R² is -0.71 against -0.82.
Ridge probes on its frozen layers give the same Kex scores as without augmentation, within the sampling noise of about 0.04. Block 4 gives R² 0.43 for both models. The largest differences are in block 3 (0.42 against 0.40) and the pooled features (0.31 against 0.25).
The perturbations cover the differences that 05_paired measured between the Bruker and Thermo spectra: broadening, shift, contrast and baseline. A model trained to ignore them still fails on the Fukushima spectra. So these measured differences are not what separates the Fukushima spectra from OSSL for Kex, or the ranges used here are too small. This run tried one setting, with each perturbation applied with probability 0.5.

title: Wet chemistry
text:
Findings
In property space, OSSL covers the Fukushima soils. No Fukushima sample is beyond OSSL’s 99th percentile of Hotelling’s T², against 1.4% of held-out OSSL samples. The median distance from a Fukushima sample to its nearest OSSL sample is 1.13 times OSSL’s own nearest-neighbour distance, against 0.99 for held-out OSSL samples. With clay as an eighth property, on 972 Fukushima samples, the ratio is the same, 1.13. On the spectra, the same ratio was 2.5 (07_inside_transfer). Each ratio compares with its own control, since the two spaces have different numbers of dimensions. Relative to those controls, the Fukushima soils are close to OSSL soils in their properties and far from them in their spectra.
The Fukushima Andosols sit a little further out (ratio 1.33), but within the T² limit, as do the OSSL Andisols (1.09). They differ from the OSSL Andisols in these properties: at the median, more exchangeable Ca (6.9 against 3.6 cmolc/kg), C (3.3 against 1.8%) and clay (20 against 7%).
The Fukushima soils span a narrower range than OSSL for every property. Their pH runs from 5.0 to 6.5 between the 5th and 95th percentiles, against 4.4 to 8.4 in OSSL.
Exchangeable K is higher in Fukushima than in OSSL, both on its own and as a share of CEC. At the median, Kex is 0.64 against 0.35 cmolc/kg, and K is 3.6% of CEC against 2.5%. For the Andosols and Andisols, K is 3.1% of CEC against 2.4%. This is consistent with potassium fertilisation after 2011, but these data don’t show the cause.
The OSSL Kex model predicts the Fukushima soils’ OSSL analogues well and the Fukushima spectra poorly. On the analogues it gives R² 0.60 (r 0.79). On the Fukushima spectra of the soils they match, it gives R² −0.76 (r 0.15). The analogues are close matches: each lies at 1.10 times the median nearest-neighbour distance among OSSL validation samples, and their Kex correlates with the Fukushima soils’ Kex at r 0.96. The CEC model shows the same pattern: R² 0.88 (r 0.94) on the analogues, against −0.67 (r 0.63) on Fukushima.
The 1,385 matches use 424 distinct Kex analogues and 453 distinct CEC analogues, since one OSSL sample can be the nearest to several Fukushima soils. The analogue scores count each OSSL sample as often as it is matched.
OSSL holds soils with properties like the Fukushima soils. From their OSSL spectra, the model predicts Kex less well than for OSSL validation samples overall (R² 0.81) or within Fukushima’s Kex range, from its minimum to its maximum (0.75), but far better than from the Fukushima spectra. These seven properties don’t describe mineralogy, such as the micas and short-range-order minerals that matter for K and Cs. Within what they measure, the zero-shot failure comes from the Fukushima spectra, through the instrument or sample preparation, and not from the soils.

text:
PCA
Each preprocessing is fitted on OSSL, then applied to the Fukushima spectra. The PCA, with 10 components, is fitted on OSSL only. T2 is Hotelling’s T², the distance within the PCA model. Q is the squared residual, the part of a spectrum the model does not explain:

pipes = {'SNV': make_pipeline(SNV()),
         'SNV + SG first derivative': make_pipeline(SNV(), SavitzkyGolay(window_length=11, polyorder=2, deriv=1))}

def fit_pca(pipe, n=10):
    Xo = pipe.fit_transform(om.spectra); Xf = pipe.transform(fuku.spectra)
    pca = PCA(n_components=n, svd_solver='randomized', random_state=0).fit(Xo)
    To, Tf = pca.transform(Xo), pca.transform(Xf)
    Eo, Ef = Xo - pca.inverse_transform(To), Xf - pca.inverse_transform(Tf)
    t2 = lambda T: (T**2 / pca.explained_variance_).sum(1)
    return dict(pca=pca, To=To, Tf=Tf, T2o=t2(To), T2f=t2(Tf), Qo=(Eo**2).sum(1), Qf=(Ef**2).sum(1), ro=(Eo**2).mean(0), rf=(Ef**2).mean(0))

title: OSSL and Fukushima spectra
text:
Findings
The figures in this section come from the tables above. They describe the current sample selection.
With SNV only, the Fukushima spectra sit away from OSSL. 22% of the Fukushima samples, and 41% of the Fukushima Andosols, are beyond the 99th percentile of OSSL’s T². The Fukushima Andosols are no closer to the OSSL Andisols than the other Fukushima soils are. Both Fukushima groups sit between 1.7 and 2.0 standard deviations below the OSSL mean on PC1, and between 2.5 and 2.8 below it on PC3. The OSSL Andisols sit at -0.75 on PC1 and +0.72 on PC3. The Andosols and the other Fukushima soils share the offset. This points to the instrument or to sample handling common to all Fukushima samples, more than to the soils.
The Savitzky-Golay first derivative removes most of the offset. No Fukushima sample is beyond OSSL’s 99th percentile of T², and 1.2% are beyond its 99th percentile of Q. An offset of about 1.5 standard deviations remains on PC2, against 0.2 for the OSSL Andisols. Most of the difference under SNV is therefore broad, such as baseline or slope.
The OSSL model leaves its largest Fukushima residuals between 3500 and 3950 cm⁻¹: 5.7 times the OSSL residual with SNV and 6.9 times with the derivative. In the quiet region from 2400 to 2800 cm⁻¹ the ratio is about 3.5. The narrow structure in 3500–3950 cm⁻¹ is not above that of the quiet region. The excess is a broad absorption, such as O–H from water held in the samples, more than water vapour lines.
Between 1300 and 2000 cm⁻¹, the Fukushima spectra have 2.1 times the narrow structure of OSSL, against 1.6 times in the quiet region. This excess is consistent with water vapour lines from the Nicolet’s beam path. The Fukushima spectra were interpolated linearly from a step of about 1.93 cm⁻¹ to 2 cm⁻¹, which smooths narrow lines a little. The narrow-structure ratios may therefore understate the Nicolet’s lines.
The CO₂ band is not a problem for Fukushima. Its spectra have less narrow structure there than OSSL (0.42 times), and the derivative model explains the band better for Fukushima than for OSSL.
The two Fukushima batches differ by about 0.8 standard deviations on PC3 with SNV. After the derivative their means differ by at most 0.12 standard deviations on each component. This notebook does not check whether the batches also differ in their soils.
Open questions for the Fukushima data team: how the samples were dried and stored before scanning, and whether the Nicolet was purged with dry air.

linear_cka is linear centred kernel alignment (Kornblith et al. 2019). It compares two representations of the same samples, which may have different numbers of features. It is 1 when one representation is a rotation and rescaling of the other, and near 0 when they are unrelated. It is computed from the n × n Gram matrices, so it works for layers with thousands of features.



linear_cka
def linear_cka(
    A, # Representation of n samples, one row per sample
    B, # Another representation of the same n samples
)->float:
Linear centred kernel alignment between A and B

Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(30, 30)))
test_close(linear_cka(A, A), 1)
test_close(linear_cka(A, 3 * A @ Q), 1)
test_eq(linear_cka(A, rng.normal(size=(200, 50))) < 0.3, True)

    Fb:dict, # The same layers for the same samples, from another model or input

title: Inside transfer
text:
Distance from a reference set
nn_ratio measures how far new samples sit from a reference set, such as Fukushima spectra from OSSL. It standardises the features on the reference set and projects them on the reference’s first n_pca principal components. It then divides the median distance from each new sample to its nearest reference sample by the median distance from each reference sample to its nearest other reference sample. A ratio near 1 means the new samples sit among the reference samples. A large ratio means they sit outside.
The ratio depends on the size of the reference set. Comparing it with the ratio for held-out samples from the reference population, which should be near 1, is a fair control.



nn_ratio
def nn_ratio(
    F_ref, # Reference representation, one row per sample
    F_new, # Representation of new samples, with the same features
    n_pca:int=50, # Number of principal components
)->float:
Median nearest-neighbour distance from F_new to F_ref, over the median within F_ref

test_eq(0.8 < nn_ratio(ref, same) < 1.3, True)
test_eq(nn_ratio(ref, shifted) > 2, True)

title: Inside transfer
text:
Findings
On Fukushima, every layer of every model holds about the same amount of linearly readable Kex information, even the model with random weights. A ridge probe on the preprocessed spectra gives a test R² of 0.33 (r 0.58). Probes on blocks 1 to 5 of all four models give 0.37 to 0.44 (r 0.61 to 0.67). The random model’s best block gives 0.41. The best probe is block 4 of the fully fine-tuned model, at 0.44. A probe on block 4 of the frozen pretrained model gives 0.43 (r 0.66), the same as the fully fine-tuned model’s own head (0.43, r 0.66). With 341 test samples, one R² has a sampling standard deviation of about 0.04, so most of these differences are within noise. In these layers, neither pretraining on OSSL nor training on Fukushima produces features that hold clearly more Kex information than random convolutions do.
On OSSL, learning makes a large difference. The pretrained model’s probes rise from 0.59 at the input to 0.79 at the pooled features, while the random model’s stay between 0.49 and 0.64. That gain does not carry over to Fukushima. There, the pretrained model’s pooled features give 0.25, less than the spectra themselves. Block 5 and the global pool are where the pretrained model turns general features into OSSL-specific ones.
The CKA comparisons point to the same split. Fine-tuning leaves blocks 1 to 4 almost unchanged (CKA with the pretrained model 0.97 or more on Fukushima spectra) and changes block 5 (0.74) and the pooled features (0.38). The Fukushima-only model is close to the pretrained model in block 1 (0.98) and moves away with depth: 0.81 in block 4, 0.50 in block 5 and 0.12 in the pooled features. The random model is also close to the pretrained model in the early blocks (0.93 in block 1), so a high CKA there mostly reflects the architecture. In block 4, the Fukushima-only model is closer to the pretrained model (0.81) than the random model is (0.68). Training on either dataset finds partly the same mid-level features.
Fukushima spectra sit outside OSSL in every layer of every model. At the input, the median distance from a Fukushima spectrum to its nearest OSSL spectrum is 2.5 times that of a held-out OSSL spectrum, whose ratio is 1.0. The random model keeps the ratio at 2.7 to 2.8 through all blocks. The trained models bring it down with depth, to about 2.0 in block 4 and 1.7 to 2.2 in block 5. None brings Fukushima among the OSSL spectra. The pretrained model’s pooled features push it back out, to 2.3.
For the 376 soils with both Bruker and Thermo spectra, the CKA between the two instruments’ representations is 0.62 at the input. In the three trained models it dips slightly in block 1 (0.59 to 0.61), rises to 0.69 to 0.73 in block 4, then falls to 0.43 to 0.51 in block 5 and 0.23 to 0.32 in the pooled features. Blocks 2 to 4 make the two instruments’ spectra of a soil more alike, and block 5 and the pool make them less alike. In the random model the CKA falls from block 1 to 0.29 in block 5, but its pooled features give 0.73. With random weights, the global average probably keeps mostly an overall intensity that both instruments share. This was not checked.
The Fukushima Kex ceiling of about 0.43 is reached by linear probes on random features, by frozen OSSL features and by the end-to-end models alike. So the limit lies in the Fukushima data rather than in the features the CNN learns. 08_learning_curve shows which part of the data: every model still gains R² with more training samples at 1,047, so the number of samples limits the scores. In the pretrained model, block 4 is the best candidate layer to transfer from. Its probe is the best of that model on Fukushima, although within noise of the others. It brings Fukushima closest to OSSL, and it makes the two instruments most alike.

title: Learning curve
text:
Findings
No model reaches a plateau. Between 700 and 1,047 training samples, the mean test R² still rises by 0.05 to 0.12 per doubling of the training set: 0.116 for the fully fine-tuned CNN, 0.088 for the Fukushima-only CNN, 0.065 for the ridge regression on block 4 and 0.048 for the ridge regression on the spectra. With 1,047 samples, the Kex scores on Fukushima are limited by the number of samples. The curve doesn’t show how far they would rise with more.
The frozen OSSL features help most when samples are few. The ridge regression on block 4 is the best model, or level with the best, at every size. At 400 samples it reaches an R² of 0.33 (r 0.57), against 0.24 for the Fukushima-only CNN, the fully fine-tuned CNN and the ridge regression on the spectra. At 1,047 samples the gap has closed: 0.43 for the ridge regression on block 4 and 0.42 for the fully fine-tuned CNN.
The fully fine-tuned CNN gains fastest from 400 samples upwards. It overtakes the Fukushima-only CNN from 700 samples (0.35 against 0.33) and leads it at 1,047 (0.42 against 0.38). At 100 samples it is unstable (R² −0.07, standard deviation 0.25 over the seeds), but its correlation (0.37) is higher than the Fukushima-only CNN’s (0.32). The schedules were chosen for 1,047 samples and not retuned for smaller sizes, so the CNNs may be underrated at small sizes.
The ridge regression on the spectra, close to a PLSR baseline, gains least: 0.33 at 1,047 samples, rising by 0.05 per doubling.

title: Al–OH band
text:
Findings
The Al–OH band near 3620 cm⁻¹ is not flattened in the Fukushima spectra. Its median second-derivative depth is 0.0104 in the Fukushima Thermo spectra, against 0.0072 in their OSSL analogues and 0.0069 in OSSL. It is deeper than in the analogue for 68% of the soils. The kaolinite band at 3695 cm⁻¹ is also deeper (0.0218 against 0.0159, in 73% of the pairs). The height above a local baseline gives the same order. For the paired soils, the Bruker spectra show the Al–OH band more deeply than the Thermo spectra (0.0119 against 0.0087), but the two instruments rank the soils alike: their depths correlate at 0.84 for the Al–OH band and 0.66 for the kaolinite band. A broad absorption hiding the band does not explain the transfer failure.
On its own, the depth of the Al–OH band does not track Kex, in OSSL either. Its Spearman correlation with Kex is -0.13 in OSSL, 0.03 in the analogues and -0.09 in the Fukushima Thermo spectra. The OSSL model’s reliance on the 3600 to 3700 cm⁻¹ region (17_importance) therefore goes through combinations with other bands, not through this band’s depth alone.
In OSSL, both bands track clay, and in Fukushima they do not. The depth of the Al–OH band correlates with clay at 0.30 in OSSL and 0.38 in the analogues of the Fukushima soils, and at -0.19 in the Fukushima Thermo spectra. For the kaolinite band, the figures are 0.46, 0.45 and -0.24. For the paired soils, the correlations with clay are near zero on both instruments: -0.08 and 0.06 for the Al–OH band on the Thermo and Bruker spectra, against 0.47 in their analogues. Because the Bruker spectra show the same loss, the instrument does not explain it.
The relation between the clay-mineral bands and the soil properties differs between Fukushima and OSSL soils with the same properties. Two explanations fit: different clay mineralogy, such as more allophane and imogolite in Andosols, which give no sharp band near 3620 cm⁻¹, or a different clay measurement, since Andosols disperse poorly and their clay content tends to be underestimated. Clay is available for 972 of the 1,385 Fukushima soils.
The split by soil type points away from the Andosols. The decoupling is strongest in the Lowland soils, the largest group, with 631 samples with clay. There, the depth of the Al–OH band correlates with clay at -0.31, and the kaolinite band at -0.35, against 0.28 and 0.39 in their analogues. With that many samples, a Spearman correlation has a standard error of about 0.04. The 146 Andosols with clay keep a weak positive relation: 0.14 for the Al–OH band and 0.06 for the kaolinite band, against 0.53 and 0.54 in their analogues. Forest and Peat soils have smaller samples and correlations of -0.11 to -0.20. In every soil type, the analogues show correlations of 0.28 to 0.64.
The Fukushima Andosols have slightly shallower bands than the Lowland soils (median Al–OH depth 0.009 against 0.011). The OSSL Andisols have much shallower bands than other OSSL soils (0.004 against 0.007), as allophane and imogolite would give. But the Fukushima Andosols are not where the relation with clay breaks most. Allophane in Andosols therefore does not explain the decoupling. In the Lowland soils, which are mostly paddy fields, more clay goes with shallower sharp clay-mineral bands. What causes this, in mineralogy or in how clay was measured, these data do not show.

12_wetchem found that the OSSL models predict OSSL soils with properties like the Fukushima soils well, and the Fukushima spectra poorly. The failure lies in the spectra. External parameter orthogonalisation (EPO; Roger et al. 2003) removes from every spectrum the directions in which spectra of the same samples differ between two measurement conditions. Here the two conditions are the Bruker and Thermo instruments of 05_paired, with whatever sample preparation each used.
The module part uses small random arrays, so it runs without the data. The sections from Paired spectra onwards read OSSL and the Fukushima data, and are marked #| fukudata.

title: EPO
text:
Projection
epo_basis takes the spectra of the same samples under two conditions, and returns the first k right singular vectors of their differences, one column per direction. The differences are not centred, so the mean difference between the conditions is part of what the directions capture. epo_project removes those directions from spectra:



epo_project
def epo_project(
    X, # Spectra, one row per sample
    V, # Directions from `epo_basis`
)->numpy.ndarray:
X with the directions V removed





epo_basis
def epo_basis(
    Xa, # Spectra under one condition, one row per sample
    Xb, # Spectra of the same samples under the other condition
    k, # Number of directions
)->numpy.ndarray: # One unit column per direction, shape (wavenumbers, k)
The first k right singular vectors of Xa - Xb



rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xa = rng.normal(size=(50, 30))
Xb = Xa + np.outer(rng.normal(size=50), np.r_[1., np.zeros(29)])
V = epo_basis(Xa, Xb, 1)
test_close(np.abs(V[:, 0]), np.r_[1., np.zeros(29)], eps=1e-8)
test_close(epo_project(Xa, V) @ V, 0, eps=1e-8)
test_close(epo_project(epo_project(Xa, V), V), epo_project(Xa, V), eps=1e-8)
test_close(epo_project(Xa, V), epo_project(Xb, V), eps=1e-8)

Paired spectra
The paired soils of 05_paired, without those in the Fukushima test set, so no test spectrum enters the correction. Both instruments’ spectra get SNV and the Savitzky-Golay first derivative. The Bruker exports end at 3996 cm⁻¹, one point short of the shared grid, so the directions are estimated on 650–3996 cm⁻¹ and the projection leaves the last point, 3998 cm⁻¹, unchanged:

Linear check
Before training a CNN, a ridge regression shows whether EPO helps at all. It trains on 20,000 random OSSL spectra with the target, after removing the first k directions, and predicts zero-shot the Fukushima spectra with the same directions removed, and 5,000 other OSSL spectra as a check that EPO keeps what OSSL needs. k = 0 is no correction. The Fukushima scores are on the training samples, which choose k, and on the test samples:

om = load_ossl().mir(wmin=shared_wns[0], wmax=shared_wns[-1])
fuku = load_fuku()
fuku.source = fuku.source.assign(Kex=fuku.source['soil_ex_K2O'] / mg_k2o_per_cmolc, CEC=fuku.source['soil_CEC'])
r = np.random.default_rng(0)
data = {}
for t, col in (('Kex', 'k.ext_usda.a725_cmolc.kg'), ('CEC', 'cec_usda.a723_cmolc.kg')):
    Xo, yo, ido = om.xy(col)
    Xf, yf, idf = fuku.xy(t)
    perm = r.permutation(len(Xo))
    data[t] = dict(Xo=pipe.fit_transform(Xo), yo=np.log1p(yo.ravel()), ido=ido, Xf=pipe.transform(Xf), yf=np.log1p(yf.ravel()),
                   is_test=np.isin(idf, test_ids), tr=perm[:20000], va=perm[20000:25000])

def zero_shot(t, V=None):
    "Scores of a ridge regression trained on OSSL for target `t`, with the directions `V` removed, or none if None"
    d = data[t]
    P = (lambda X: X) if V is None else (lambda X: epo_project(X, V))

Analogue EPO
The paired Bruker spectra fail with the OSSL models too, so correcting towards them cannot work. The soil analogues of 12_wetchem give pairs with OSSL itself: each Fukushima soil and the OSSL sample with the closest properties. The two soils of a pair are not the same, so their spectral differences mix soil variation with the difference in measurement. title: EPO
text:
Findings
EPO with the paired Bruker and Thermo spectra doesn’t make OSSL models transfer to Fukushima. With a ridge regression trained on OSSL, the zero-shot correlation for Fukushima Kex stays between −0.09 and 0.04 for every number of removed directions from 0 to 32, on the training and the test samples. For CEC it varies between 0.35 and 0.55 without a consistent gain over no correction (0.50 on the training samples, 0.47 on the test samples). The OSSL validation R² stays at 0.65 for Kex and 0.96 for CEC, so the projection keeps what OSSL needs, but it doesn’t fix Fukushima. All Fukushima R² values are negative, from large biases.
The 365 paired soils give a clear structure: the first direction holds 80% of the squared differences, and 8 directions hold 94%.
A likely reason is in 05_paired. The OSSL Kex model fails on the Bruker spectra of these soils too (correlation 0.19). EPO removes how the Thermo spectra differ from these Bruker spectra. Even a perfect correction would only bring the Thermo spectra to the Bruker spectra, which are themselves not like OSSL’s for Kex. The Bruker instrument and preparation behind these exports are not known, and may differ from those of the KSSL spectra in OSSL.
EPO from the soil analogues doesn’t fix the transfer either. Its 1,045 pairs per target use about 690 distinct OSSL analogues. The first direction holds 68% of the squared differences, and 8 directions hold 91%. Removing them reduces the Kex bias: the Fukushima R² rises from −20 to −22 without correction to between −2 and −3 for 4 directions or more. The correlation stays low: at most 0.16 on the training samples and 0.10 on the test samples. For CEC, 4 directions give the best correlation, 0.55 on the training samples and 0.51 on the test samples, against 0.50 and 0.47 without correction. More directions lower it.
Neither linear correction, towards the Bruker spectra or towards OSSL analogues, gives the ridge regression a usable zero-shot correlation for Kex. Pretraining the CNN on EPO-projected OSSL spectra was not run, because the linear checks give no reason to expect a gain.

The 1,389 samples of the current selection come from 391 fields, and most fields were sampled in several years. In the Cs137 study’s split, used by every notebook so far, 89% of the 398 test samples come from a field that also has samples in training. A model can then partly recognise the field rather than predict from the soil, which favours models trained on Fukushima labels and can hide what OSSL adds for new fields.
This notebook scores the models with 5-fold cross-validation in which all samples of a field are in the same fold, and compares this with ordinary shuffled 5-fold cross-validation of the same samples. Every sample gets one out-of-fold prediction, so the scores by soil type and field type use all samples, not only the 341 of the fixed test set.

title: Grouped cross-validation by field

Folds
The folds come from soilspecdl’s group_folds, which gives every sample of a group the same fold. Groups are dealt to folds in random order, so folds hold about the same number of groups.

title: Grouped cross-validation by field

Out-of-fold predictions
oof_preds fits an estimator on all folds but one and predicts the one left out, for each fold. Within each training set, GridSearchCV chooses the hyperparameters on inner folds made by group_folds from the same groups, so no field is in both the inner training and validation sets either:

    est, # Unfitted scikit-learn estimator
    grid:dict, # Parameter grid for `GridSearchCV`
    X, # Features, one row per sample

    groups, # Group of each sample, used for the inner folds
    k:int=5, # Number of inner folds

Out-of-fold predictions of est, with hyperparameters chosen by inner cross-validation grouped by groups

title: Grouped cross-validation by field
text:
Findings
Knowing the field inflated every earlier score. With shuffled folds, which like the Cs137 study’s split put most fields in both training and test, ridge on the spectra reaches R² 0.38 for Kex and 0.58 for the Cs-137 ratio. With folds grouped by field, it reaches 0.28 and 0.52. Ridge on block 4 of the OSSL Kex and CEC models drops more, from 0.40 to 0.26 for Kex and from 0.66 to 0.57 for the ratio.
For Kex, the OSSL features add nothing on new fields. Over all samples, their R² gain over ridge on the spectra is -0.015 (95% interval -0.055 to 0.027). With shuffled folds it is 0.019 (-0.017 to 0.055). So the small OSSL gain in the earlier notebooks partly came from recognising fields.
For the Cs-137 ratio, frozen OSSL features help on new fields, but only slightly. All three models below use ridge regression, scored with folds grouped by field; only the input changes. Ridge on the preprocessed spectra (SNV, then a Savitzky-Golay first derivative) gives R² 0.52. Ridge on block 4 of the OSSL Kex and CEC models, with their weights frozen, gives R² 0.57, a gain of 0.047 (0.017 to 0.077). Ridge on block 4 of the same models with random weights gains -0.009. The gain therefore comes from OSSL pretraining, not from the network architecture. It cuts the unexplained variance from 48% to 43%. With shuffled folds, the random-weights model gains too. This revises 10_cs137, where the random model took most of the gain on a split that shares fields.
No soil type holds the weak Kex transfer on its own. OSSL features give no clear gain in any soil type, and their gain is above zero only in Lowland paddy fields: 0.079 (0.015 to 0.146), from an R² of 0.02 to 0.10. In Andosols, which OSSL’s Andisols might be expected to help, the gain is -0.056 (-0.199 to 0.054).
Kex is barely predictable within paddy fields. On new fields, ridge on the spectra gives R² -0.03 in paddy fields (880 samples) and 0.20 in upland fields (505). In Lowland paddy fields it gives 0.02, and in Andosol paddy fields -0.39. Much of the overall R² of 0.28 therefore comes from telling paddy from upland samples, not from ranking samples within either. Paddy fields hold 63% of the samples. Whether their Kex reflects added K fertiliser, which leaves no mineral signature in the spectra, is a question for the Fukushima data team.
The Cs-137 ratio is predictable in every large group, with R² 0.48 to 0.60 on new fields in paddy and upland fields and in Lowland soils. The OSSL gain is about 0.05 in each of these groups. It is largest in Andosols, at 0.12 (-0.035 to 0.374) on new fields and 0.17 (0.069 to 0.351) with shuffled folds. PLSR beats ridge on the spectra in Forest soils, by 0.11 (0.047 to 0.221).
Groups of fewer than about 70 samples, which are Peat, Red-yellow and Gley soils, have R² intervals too wide to compare models. Their percentile intervals can even leave out the point estimate, because R² on a resample of a few fields is biased low.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
from fastcore.test import *

Water vapour in the beam of an FTIR spectrometer adds many narrow lines, in the H–O–H bending region (about 1300–2000 cm⁻¹) and the O–H stretching region (about 3500–3950 cm⁻¹). No soil component gives lines that narrow. A spectrum is the sample scan against a background scan, so the lines can point up, if the sample scan had more vapour, or down, if the background had more. 01_pca found more narrow structure in the Fukushima spectra than in OSSL between 1300 and 2000 cm⁻¹.
The replicate scans of a sample measure the same soil. Their differences hold the measurement differences, such as vapour and noise, and no soil differences. They show the vapour pattern most clearly.
The module part uses small random arrays, so it runs without the data. The sections from Native grid onwards read OSSL and the Fukushima data, and are marked #| fukudata.

title: Water vapour
text:
Functions
highpass keeps the narrow structure of each spectrum: the spectrum minus a Savitzky-Golay smooth with a window of window points. On the 2 cm⁻¹ grid, 11 points is 22 cm⁻¹, narrower than most soil bands and wider than vapour lines. band_mask marks the wavenumbers in bands:



band_mask
def band_mask(
    wns, # Wavenumbers
    bands:list=[(1300, 2000), (3500, 3950)], # (low, high) ranges, in cm⁻¹
)->numpy.ndarray: # True for the wavenumbers in any of `bands`
Mask of the wavenumbers within bands





highpass

    window:int=11, # Window of the Savitzky-Golay smooth, in points, odd
    polyorder:int=2, # Degree of the smoothing polynomial

X minus its Savitzky-Golay smooth


replicate_deviations subtracts from each replicate the mean of its sample’s replicates, for samples with at least two. vapour_pattern returns the first principal component of high-passed spectra within mask, as a unit vector that is zero outside mask, with its sign set so that its largest entry is positive. It also returns that component’s share of the variance within mask. vapour_score projects the high-passed spectra on a pattern:



vapour_score

    X, # Spectra, one per row, on the wavenumbers of `v`
    v, # Pattern from `vapour_pattern`
    window:int=11, # Passed to `highpass`

title: Water vapour
text:
Findings
The Fukushima spectra contain a clear water-vapour pattern. The .spa files have a point spacing of 1.93 cm⁻¹, so the 2 cm⁻¹ grid keeps their narrow structure. The pattern estimated from replicate deviations and the one estimated from the averaged sample spectra correlate at r 0.99. In the vapour bands, the first component holds 26% of the narrow-structure variance of the replicate deviations, where noise holds much of the rest, and 60% of that of the sample spectra.
The Fukushima vapour lines are about twice as strong as OSSL’s, and mostly point down. The median absolute score is 0.0033 for Fukushima and 0.0015 for OSSL, and the 95th percentiles are 0.013 and 0.005. 95% of the Fukushima scores are below 0.0003, so their background scans almost always held more vapour than their sample scans. The scores of a sample’s replicates spread much less than the scores vary between samples (median spread 0.0002), so the vapour level was set per session rather than per scan. Batch 1 has more vapour than batch 2 (mean score −0.0056 against −0.0032). The year makes less difference.
Vapour doesn’t explain the transfer failure. Its Spearman correlation with the Kex errors is at most 0.09 in absolute value: for the zero-shot error of the OSSL model, and for the residuals of the fully fine-tuned and Fukushima-only models. The OSSL model fails zero-shot on the quarter of the samples with the least vapour too (correlation 0.19, R² −0.60). On the quarter with the most vapour, the correlation is 0.08. The four quarters show no steady trend.
The score measures the narrow vapour lines only. Water held by the soil gives broad bands, near 3400 and 1630 cm⁻¹, which highpass removes. This notebook doesn’t test that.

title: Multi-task pretraining
text:
Findings
The multi-task model learns all 23 properties on OSSL. Its validation R² ranges from 0.62 for extractable P to 0.99 for total carbon, and is 0.90 or more for 12 of the 23 tasks. For Kex it is 0.75, slightly below the single-task model’s 0.79, on a different random validation set.
Its frozen layers transfer to Fukushima no better than those of the single-task models. The best layer of each model gives these test R²:

Kex: 0.43 for the multi-task model (block 2) and the Kex model (block 4), and 0.44 for the Kex and CEC models together;
CEC: 0.74 for the multi-task model, 0.75 for the Kex model, and 0.75 for the Kex and CEC models together;
Cs-137 ratio: 0.62 for the multi-task model, 0.64 for the Kex model, and 0.66 for the Kex and CEC models together (block 5).

With 341 test samples, one R² has a sampling standard deviation of about 0.04, so these differences are within noise. With 200 and 400 training samples, block 4 of the multi-task model scores within 0.03 of the single-task models for every target.
At their best layer with all training samples, the pretrained models beat random weights by 0.00 to 0.05; the CEC model’s best layer for Kex is level with random. With 200 or 400 training samples, block 4 of every pretrained model beats random weights by 0.04 to 0.08 for Kex and the Cs-137 ratio.
Which OSSL properties a model learns makes little difference to how well its frozen layers serve Fukushima. With these pretraining data, the transfer seems limited by how far Fukushima spectra sit from OSSL (07_inside_transfer), not by the pretraining objective.
